lesson.title: The Nerve Impulse Itself: Inside the Action Potential
lesson.summary: The action potential is the brief, self-propagating electrical spike that races down a neuron's axon once depolarization reaches threshold, serving as the actual signal that carries information from one end of a neuron to the other.
lesson.body:
Depolarization, as covered previously, pushes a neuron's membrane potential up from its resting negative 70 millivolts toward threshold, typically around negative 55 millivolts. Reaching that threshold is not a minor event, it triggers the action potential: a rapid, dramatic spike in voltage that is the actual nerve impulse traveling down the axon.

At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels along the axon snap open, distinct from the channels involved in ordinary depolarization at the dendrites. Na+ floods into the cell so quickly that it creates a positive feedback loop, more Na+ entering causes more depolarization, which opens still more Na+ channels, driving the voltage rapidly upward until it peaks around positive 30 to 40 millivolts, briefly reversing the cell's normal polarity so the inside becomes positive relative to the outside. At that peak, the Na+ channels inactivate, essentially locking shut, while voltage-gated potassium channels open, letting K+ rush out of the cell and driving the voltage back down toward negative, a phase called repolarization. The K+ channels often stay open slightly too long, briefly overshooting past resting potential into a more negative hyperpolarized dip before the membrane settles back to its normal negative 70 millivolt baseline.

The action potential follows the all-or-none principle directly: once threshold is crossed, the resulting spike is essentially identical in size every time, regardless of how much stronger the triggering stimulus was. If threshold is not reached, no action potential fires at all, there is no smaller or partial version. It is often compared to flushing a toilet, pressing the handle harder does not produce a bigger flush, once the mechanism is triggered the same full response happens.

An action potential does not just occur once and stay put, it self-propagates down the entire length of the axon. Each depolarized patch of membrane triggers the neighboring patch to reach threshold in turn, so the impulse moves like a wave of falling dominoes toward the axon terminals. In myelinated axons this movement is accelerated further through saltatory conduction, with the signal effectively jumping between the nodes of Ranvier described earlier in neural transmission, letting a reflex signal travel from the spinal cord to a distant muscle in a fraction of a second, exactly the kind of speed the withdrawal reflex depends on.

A concrete example is a motor neuron firing to trigger a muscle twitch: once its axon hillock crosses threshold, an identical action potential barrels down its axon to the muscle every time, regardless of exactly how strong the original triggering input was, whether that input came from a gentle tap or a firm push. But the neuron cannot immediately repeat this feat. The Na+ channels that just fired need a moment to reset, so right after firing, the neuron enters a brief period where it resists or cannot fire again, the refractory period, which is the next piece of this picture.
